children: The bank’s existing and new cardholders will automatically get zero forex markup on international transactions without any upgrade or spending requirement

IDFC FIRST Bank has removed foreign exchange markup charges across its entire credit card portfolio, allowing existing and new customers to make eligible international transactions without paying the additional forex fee.

The benefit is being extended automatically to all credit card customers, with no requirement to apply for a new card, upgrade an existing card or meet a minimum spending threshold. It covers international transactions such as overseas purchases, online payments, subscriptions and other eligible foreign-currency spends.
Zero Forex Markup Across Card Portfolio

Forex markup is an additional charge levied by card issuers when a transaction is made in a foreign currency. Depending on the card, the charge can range from 1 per cent to 3.5 per cent, with Goods and Services Tax applicable on the fee.

Under the new structure, the bank has removed this markup across its credit card portfolio. The move extends the zero-markup proposition beyond premium and travel-focused cards to a wider set of customers.

The bank has also clarified that the zero-markup benefit does not mean every cost associated with an international transaction is waived. Exchange rates, merchant charges, ATM fees and other transaction-specific costs may still apply.
Customers Can Continue Using Existing Cards
Customers do not need to switch to a new credit card to access the benefit. The change applies to both existing and new cardholders.

The bank has also said applicable Reward Points or cashback will continue under the respective card programmes, although the treatment of international transactions is subject to the terms applicable to individual cards.

Customers making payments overseas should also be mindful of dynamic currency conversion. Choosing to pay in the local currency generally allows the transaction to be processed under the card's foreign-currency conversion terms, while choosing Indian rupees at an overseas merchant or ATM can involve a separate conversion charge.
The move comes as Indian banks and fintech companies increasingly compete on international spending benefits, particularly as overseas travel and cross-border online purchases gain traction.
